question: The Italian health sector comprises around 30 health professions, all of which are: intellectually challenging, demand accountability and require a university degree, membership of a professional body and continuous training. Only eight categories (e.g. doctors and psychologists, etc.)

can occupy a permanent public post and also run regular private practices, while the remaining 22 (around 600 000 professionals) are de facto precluded from doing this. In view also of the CJEU judgment of 13 January 2022 in Case C-282/19, can the Commission state whether: 1.

Discrimination may exist between Italian professionals in the same health sector, in breach of Articles 4 and 18 of Directive 2000/78/EC, Articles 1 and 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and/or of Article 153 TFEU?
Whether it is aware of potential discrimination between Italian healthcare professionals and workers from other EU countries who do the same jobs?
answer: Council Directive 2000/78/EC prohibits discrimination in employment, including as regards working conditions, on the grounds of religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation (1). The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) clarified that its scope may not be extended beyond the listed ground s (2).

From the facts provided in the Honourable Member’s question, there seem to be no indications that possible less favourable treatment or particular disadvantages in the situation referred to would relate specifically to any of those grounds. As regards the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, it applies to Member States when they are implementing EU law (3).

There are no indications to that effect in the Honourable Member’s question. Likewise, there seems to be no breach of Article 153 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), as the function of this provision is rather to set the power of the Union to support the Member States in the promotion of employment, improved living and working conditions.

Enshrined in Article 45 TFEU, the freedom of movement for workers entails the prohibition of discrimination based on nationality between workers of the Member States in employment, remuneration and other conditions of work.

It is settled case-law of the CJEU that the concept of discrimination covers not only direct discrimination on grounds of nationality but also all forms of indirect discrimination which lead to the same result. The Commission is not aware of cases of discrimination between Italian and EU workers in the healthcare sector.

Council Directive 2000/78/EC of 27 November 2000 establishing a general framework for equal treatment in employment and occupation, OJ L 303, 2.12.2000, p. 16-22, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32000L0078 See, for example: judgment of 11 July 2006, Chacón Navas, C-13/05, ECLI:EU:C:2006:456. Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, Article 51(1).
